metadata.title: Heights and the specialization map for Families of elliptic curves over $\PP^n$

nodes.name: Theorem A
nodes.statement: Given any $P \in E(K)$, there exists a set $B_P$ consisting of a finite number of codimension-two subvarieties in $\PP^n$, such that if $\G \subset \PP^n$ is a smooth hypersurface that does not contain any subvariety in $B_P$ and $E_\G/\CQ(\G)$ is non-singular, then $$\frac{\hat{h}_{E_\G}(P_\G)}{\deg \G}= \hat{h}_E(P). $$
nodes.statement_short: For every $P \in E(K)$ the ratio $\hat{h}_{E_\G}(P_\G)/\deg \G$ equals $\hat{h}_E(P)$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\G$ avoiding a fixed finite set $B_P$ of codimension-two subvarieties.
assumptions: Given any $P \in E(K)$
$\G \subset \PP^n$ is a smooth hypersurface that does not contain any subvariety in $B_P$ and $E_\G/\CQ(\G)$ is non-singular
conclusions: $$\frac{\hat{h}_{E_\G}(P_\G)}{\deg \G}= \hat{h}_E(P). $$

nodes.name: Theorem B
nodes.statement: With notations as explained above and let $d \geq 1$ be a fixed integer, then there exist infinitely many smooth curves $C/\CQ$ of degree $d$ in $\PP^n$ that do not lie in the complement of $U$ and such that the set $$\{ t \in C(\CQ) \cap U(\CQ) \ | \ \s_t \text{ is not injective }\} $$ is a set of bounded height. Furthermore, the union of all such curves is Zariski dense in $\PP^n$.
nodes.statement_short: For each degree $d$ there are infinitely many smooth curves $C \subset \PP^n$ on which $\s_t$ fails to be injective only for $t$ of bounded height, and their union is Zariski dense.
assumptions: With notations as explained above and let $d \geq 1$ be a fixed integer
conclusions: there exist infinitely many smooth curves $C/\CQ$ of degree $d$ in $\PP^n$ that do not lie in the complement of $U$ and such that the set $$\{ t \in C(\CQ) \cap U(\CQ) \ | \ \s_t \text{ is not injective }\} $$ is a set of bounded height
the union of all such curves is Zariski dense in $\PP^n$

the union of all such curves is Zariski dense in $\PP^n$

nodes.name: Néron's theorem on injectivity of the specialization map
nodes.statement: In the setting of general abelian varieties over $K=k(\PP^n)$ for any number field $k$, N\'eron (\cite{NPA}) proved that there are infinitely many $t \in \PP^n(k)$ such that $\s_t$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: For abelian varieties over $k(\PP^n)$ there are infinitely many $k$-points $t$ with injective specialization map.
assumptions: In the setting of general abelian varieties over $K=k(\PP^n)$ for any number field $k$
conclusions: there are infinitely many $t \in \PP^n(k)$ such that $\s_t$ is injective

nodes.name: Masser's theorem on specializations of finitely generated subgroups
nodes.statement: Later, Masser (\cite{MSF}) proved a stronger result in a more general setting of abelian varieties $A$ defined over $K=k(V)$, the function field of a projective variety $V$ defined over a number field $k$. Masser proved that the specialization map $\s_t$ is ``almost always'' injective by showing that the set of $t \in V(k)$ with Weil height bounded by $h$ and such that $\s_t$ is not injective lies on a hypersurface of degree bounded by a constant power of $h$.
nodes.statement_short: The non-injective specializations of bounded Weil height lie on a hypersurface of degree polynomially bounded in the height.
assumptions: abelian varieties $A$ defined over $K=k(V)$, the function field of a projective variety $V$ defined over a number field $k$
conclusions: the specialization map $\s_t$ is ``almost always'' injective
the set of $t \in V(k)$ with Weil height bounded by $h$ and such that $\s_t$ is not injective lies on a hypersurface of degree bounded by a constant power of $h$

nodes.name: Silverman's Theorem C
nodes.statement: Moreover, in the case where $V=C$ is a smooth curve, Silverman (\cite{SHS}, Theorem C) proved that the set of $t \in C(\overline{k})$ for which $\s_t$ is not injective is a set of bounded height.
assumptions: in the case where $V=C$ is a smooth curve
conclusions: the set of $t \in C(\overline{k})$ for which $\s_t$ is not injective is a set of bounded height

nodes.name: Silverman's Theorem B
nodes.statement: Silverman (\cite{SHS}, Theorem B) proved that for $\pi : A\longrightarrow C$, a family of abelian varieties over a smooth curve, we have $$\lim_{\substack{t \in C(\CQ) \\ h_{C}(t) \rightarrow \infty} } \frac{\hat{h}_{A_{t}}(P_{t})}{h_{C}(t)} = \hat{h}_{A_\eta}(P_\eta), $$ where $A_\eta/\CQ(C)$ is the generic fiber of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: For a family of abelian varieties over a smooth curve, the specialized canonical height divided by the base Weil height tends to the canonical height on the generic fiber.
assumptions: for $\pi : A\longrightarrow C$, a family of abelian varieties over a smooth curve
conclusions: $$\lim_{\substack{t \in C(\CQ) \\ h_{C}(t) \rightarrow \infty} } \frac{\hat{h}_{A_{t}}(P_{t})}{h_{C}(t)} = \hat{h}_{A_\eta}(P_\eta), $$ where $A_\eta/\CQ(C)$ is the generic fiber of $A$

nodes.name: Bézout's theorem
nodes.statement: by B\'ezout's theorem, we get $\deg \iota_\G^* (f_P^{-1}(L)) = \deg \G \cdot \deg f_P^{-1}(L)$

nodes.name: Lang, Chapter 3, Proposition 3.2 (Weil height as the degree of a hyperplane pull-back)
nodes.statement: (Lang \cite{LFD} Chapter 3, Proposition 3.2 ) Let $V$ be a projective variety in $\PP^n$, non-singular in codimension one, defined over a number field $k$, and let $P$ be a point in the projective space $\PP^r$, rational over $k(V)$. Let $f_P:V \dashrightarrow \PP^r$ be the rational map defined over $k$, determined by $P$. Then $$h_{\PP^r(\bar{k}(V))}(P)=\deg f_P^{-1}(L) $$for any hyperplane $L$ of $\PP^r$, such that $ f_P^{-1}(L)$ is defined, the degree being that in the given projective embedding of $V$ in $\PP^n$.
nodes.origin_citation: Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapter 3, Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement_short: The Weil height of a $k(V)$-rational point of $\PP^r$ equals the degree of the pull-back of a hyperplane under the rational map it induces.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a projective variety in $\PP^n$, non-singular in codimension one, defined over a number field $k$, and let $P$ be a point in the projective space $\PP^r$, rational over $k(V)$
Let $f_P:V \dashrightarrow \PP^r$ be the rational map defined over $k$, determined by $P$
conclusions: $$h_{\PP^r(\bar{k}(V))}(P)=\deg f_P^{-1}(L) $$for any hyperplane $L$ of $\PP^r$, such that $ f_P^{-1}(L)$ is defined, the degree being that in the given projective embedding of $V$ in $\PP^n$

nodes.name: Positive definiteness of the canonical height pairing
nodes.statement: In general, $\< \cdot , \cdot \>_E$ is positive definite on the quotient of $E(K)$ by the subgroup generated by $E(K)_\text{tors}$ and $K/\CQ\text{-trace of }E(K)$ (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 5.4).
nodes.origin_citation: Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapter 6, Theorem 5.4
conclusions: $\< \cdot , \cdot \>_E$ is positive definite on the quotient of $E(K)$ by the subgroup generated by $E(K)_\text{tors}$ and $K/\CQ\text{-trace of }E(K)$

nodes.name: Codimension of the indeterminacy locus and invariance of the divisor class group
nodes.statement: In general, if we have a rational map $f : V \dashrightarrow W$ between projective varieties and $V$ is non-singular, the indeterminacy locus of $f$, which we denote as $I_f$, has codimension at least $2$ (\cite{SAT} Chapter III, Proposition 3.5b) and so we have the following isomorphism (\cite{HAG} Chapter II, Proposition 6.5b) of divisor class groups induced by the inclusion $j:U:= V\backslash I_f \longhookrightarrow V$: \begin{align*} j^*: \Pic(V) &\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \Pic(U)\\ c &\longmapsto c \cap U \end{align*}with projective closure in $V$ as the inverse homomorphism.
nodes.origin_citation: Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Chapter III, Proposition 3.5b; Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Chapter II, Proposition 6.5b
nodes.statement_short: The indeterminacy locus of a rational map from a non-singular variety has codimension $\geq 2$, so restriction induces an isomorphism $\Pic(V) \cong \Pic(V \setminus I_f)$.
assumptions: if we have a rational map $f : V \dashrightarrow W$ between projective varieties and $V$ is non-singular
conclusions: the indeterminacy locus of $f$, which we denote as $I_f$, has codimension at least $2$
we have the following isomorphism (\cite{HAG} Chapter II, Proposition 6.5b) of divisor class groups induced by the inclusion $j:U:= V\backslash I_f \longhookrightarrow V$

nodes.name: Functoriality of pull-backs of divisor classes
nodes.statement: Pull-backs are functorial on the category of varieties (\cite{FIT} Chapter 2, Section 2.2, \cite{HAG} Appendix A, Theorem 1.1), so for any divisor class $c \in \Pic(\PP^r)$, we have $$\iota_{\G^o}^*(f|_{U^o}^*(c))=(f|_{U^o} \circ \iota_{\G^o})^*(c). $$
nodes.origin_citation: Fulton, Intersection Theory, Chapter 2, Section 2.2; Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Appendix A, Theorem 1.1
assumptions: for any divisor class $c \in \Pic(\PP^r)$
conclusions: Pull-backs are functorial on the category of varieties

nodes.name: Finiteness of $E(K)/E_0(K)$ via the Néron model
nodes.statement: Thus, the smooth part of the Weierstrass model gives the N\'eron model of $E/K$ and the quotient group $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite (\cite{SAT} Chapter IV, Corollary 9.2d).
nodes.origin_citation: Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Chapter IV, Corollary 9.2d
assumptions: With the minimality assumption on the Weierstrass equation, $E/K$ is defined by a Weierstrass equation with coefficients in $\Ocal_\G$ and minimal with respect to the prime divisor $\G$
conclusions: the smooth part of the Weierstrass model gives the N\'eron model of $E/K$ and the quotient group $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite

nodes.name: Lemma 2 (pull-back of divisor classes commutes with restriction to a hypersurface)
nodes.statement: For $n\geq 2$, let $f : \PP^n \dashrightarrow \PP^r$ be a rational map and $\G \stackrel{\iota}{\longhookrightarrow} \PP^n$ be a smooth hypersurface, where all the varieties are defined over an algebraically closed field $k$. Suppose $\G$ does not contain any codimension-two component of the indeterminacy locus of $f$, then $$(f \circ \iota)^{-1}(c)=\iota^*(f^{-1}(c)), $$ for any divisor class $c \in \Pic(\PP^r)$.
nodes.statement_short: If a smooth hypersurface $\G$ misses every codimension-two component of $I_f$, then pulling back a divisor class along $f \circ \iota$ agrees with restricting $f^{-1}(c)$ to $\G$.
assumptions: For $n\geq 2$, let $f : \PP^n \dashrightarrow \PP^r$ be a rational map and $\G \stackrel{\iota}{\longhookrightarrow} \PP^n$ be a smooth hypersurface, where all the varieties are defined over an algebraically closed field $k$
Suppose $\G$ does not contain any codimension-two component of the indeterminacy locus of $f$
conclusions: $$(f \circ \iota)^{-1}(c)=\iota^*(f^{-1}(c)), $$ for any divisor class $c \in \Pic(\PP^r)$

nodes.name: Lemma 3 (Weil height under reduction modulo a hypersurface)
nodes.statement: Let $f_P : \PP^n \dashrightarrow \PP^2$ be the rational map induced by $P \in E(K)$ with indeterminacy locus $I_{f_P}$. If $\G \stackrel{\iota}{\longhookrightarrow} \PP^n$ is a smooth hypersurface such that $E_\G$ is non-singular and $\G$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_{f_P}$, then \begin{equation}\frac{h_{E_\G}(P_\G)}{\deg \G}= h_E(P). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For a smooth hypersurface $\G$ with $E_\G$ non-singular and missing the codimension-two components of $I_{f_P}$, one has $h_{E_\G}(P_\G)/\deg \G = h_E(P)$.
assumptions: Let $f_P : \PP^n \dashrightarrow \PP^2$ be the rational map induced by $P \in E(K)$ with indeterminacy locus $I_{f_P}$
$\G \stackrel{\iota}{\longhookrightarrow} \PP^n$ is a smooth hypersurface such that $E_\G$ is non-singular and $\G$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_{f_P}$
conclusions: \begin{equation}\frac{h_{E_\G}(P_\G)}{\deg \G}= h_E(P). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Lemma 4 (specialization commutes with duplication)
nodes.statement: For $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H_\infty$ such that the specialized point $P_t:=f_P(t)=[x(t):y(t):z(t)]$ is a non-singular point on the specialized (possibly singular) cubic curve $E_t$ defined by \begin{equation} Y^2Z=X^3+A(t)XZ^2+B(t)Z^3, \end{equation} $([2]P)_t=f_{[2]P}(t)$ is also well-defined and $([2]P)_t=[2]P_t$.
nodes.statement_short: If $P_t$ is a non-singular point of the specialized cubic $E_t$, then $([2]P)_t$ is defined and equals $[2]P_t$.
assumptions: For $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H_\infty$ such that the specialized point $P_t:=f_P(t)=[x(t):y(t):z(t)]$ is a non-singular point on the specialized (possibly singular) cubic curve $E_t$
conclusions: $([2]P)_t=f_{[2]P}(t)$ is also well-defined and $([2]P)_t=[2]P_t$

nodes.name: Lemma 5 (non-singular reduction after multiplication by $N$)
nodes.statement: With the minimality of the Weierstrass equation that defines $E/K$, for any $P \in E(K)$, there exists a natural number $N$ such that $([N]P)_\G$ is not a singular point on $E_\G(\CQ(\G))$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\G \neq H_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Some fixed multiple $[N]P$ reduces to a non-singular point modulo every smooth hypersurface $\G \neq H_\infty$.
assumptions: With the minimality of the Weierstrass equation that defines $E/K$
for any $P \in E(K)$
conclusions: there exists a natural number $N$ such that $([N]P)_\G$ is not a singular point on $E_\G(\CQ(\G))$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\G \neq H_\infty$

nodes.name: Lemma 6 (trichotomy at points of $H_\infty$ outside $H'_\infty$)
nodes.statement: Let $t=[0,1:*:\ldots:*] \in H_\infty(\CQ) \backslash H'_\infty(\CQ)$ such that the rational map $f_P$ is not defined at $t$. Then exactly one of the following statements is true: \begin{itemize} \item[a)] $f_{P'}$ is not defined at $t$, \item[b)] $P'_t$ is a singular point on $E'_t(\CQ)$, \item[c)] $P'_t$ is a torsion point of order $2$ on $E'_t(\CQ)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: At a point of $H_\infty \setminus H'_\infty$ where $f_P$ is undefined, exactly one of three alternatives holds for $P'$: $f_{P'}$ undefined, $P'_t$ singular, or $P'_t$ of order $2$.
assumptions: Let $t=[0,1:*:\ldots:*] \in H_\infty(\CQ) \backslash H'_\infty(\CQ)$ such that the rational map $f_P$ is not defined at $t$
conclusions: Then exactly one of the following statements is true
$f_{P'}$ is not defined at $t$
$P'_t$ is a singular point on $E'_t(\CQ)$
$P'_t$ is a torsion point of order $2$ on $E'_t(\CQ)$

nodes.name: Weil height on $\PP^r(\bar{k}(V))$
nodes.statement: For any $P=[f_0: \ldots: f_r]$ in $\PP^r(\bar{k}(V))$, the Weil height of $P$ is given by $$h_{\PP^r(\bar{k}(V))}(P):= \sum_{\G} \max_i\{-\ord_{\G}(f_i)\}\deg_\phi(\G), $$ where the summation is taken over all prime divisors in $\Div_{\bar{k}}(V)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapter 3
nodes.statement_short: Weil height of a $\bar{k}(V)$-rational point of $\PP^r$: the sum over prime divisors of the maximal pole order times the divisor degree.

nodes.name: Degree map $\deg_\phi$ on divisors
nodes.statement: We fix a closed embedding $\phi : V \longhookrightarrow \PP^n$ and thus the degree map $\deg_\phi$ is well-defined on $\Div_{\bar{k}}(V)$, i.e. for any prime divisor $D \in \Div_{\bar{k}}(V)$, $\deg_\phi (D)$ is the degree of the projective subvariety $\phi(D)$ in $\PP^n$ and we extend it linearly to all divisors.
nodes.statement_short: Degree of a prime divisor $D$ of $V$ measured as the degree of $\phi(D)$ in $\PP^n$, extended linearly.

nodes.name: Weil height $h_E$ on $E(k(V))$
nodes.statement: Let $E/k(V)$ be an elliptic curve over the function field $k(V)$ defined by a Weierstrass equation and $O$ be the zero element. Then this embedding of $E$ into $\PP^2_{k(V)}$ is induced by the very ample divisor $3(O)$. Let $h_E$ be the Weil height corresponds to this embedding, i.e. for any $P=[x:y:z] \in E(k(V))$, $$h_E(P)=h_{\PP^2(k(V))}([x:y:z]). $$
nodes.origin_citation: Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapters 3, 4
nodes.statement_short: Weil height on an elliptic curve over $k(V)$, taken through the Weierstrass embedding induced by $3(O)$.
nodes.definiendum: the Weil height corresponds to this embedding

nodes.name: Canonical height $\hat{h}_E$ induced by $(O)$
nodes.statement: Since the divisor $3(O)$ is even, the canonical height $\hat{h}_E$ induced by $(O)$ is defined by $$\hat{h}_{E}(P):=\frac{1}{3}\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\frac{h_{E}([n]P)}{n^2}. $$
nodes.origin_citation: Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapter 5
nodes.statement_short: Canonical height as one third of the limit of $h_E([n]P)/n^2$.

nodes.name: Pull-back $f^{-1}$ of a divisor class along a rational map
nodes.statement: Given a rational map $f : V \dashrightarrow W$ between projective varieties and $V$ is non-singular. Denote $I_f$ to be the indeterminacy locus of $f$ and $U:= V\backslash I_f$. Let $j: U \longhookrightarrow V$ be the inclusion map and $f|_{U}:U\longrightarrow W$ be the restriction of $f$ on $U$, which is a morphism between quasi-projective varieties. Then $f|_{U}^* : \Pic(W) \longrightarrow \Pic(U)$ is well-defined and we define $f^{-1}:=(j^*)^{-1} \circ f|_{U}^* : \Pic(W) \longrightarrow \Pic(V)$, i.e. $f^{-1}$ is defined such that the following diagram commutes: $$\xymatrix{ &\Pic(U) &\Pic(W) \ar@{->}[l]_{f|_{U}^*} \ar@{->}[dl]^{f^{-1}} \\ &\Pic(V) \ar@{->}[u]^{j^*}_\cong }$$
nodes.statement_short: For a rational map $f$ from a non-singular $V$, define $f^{-1} := (j^*)^{-1} \circ f|_U^*$ using the isomorphism $\Pic(V) \cong \Pic(U)$ with $U = V \setminus I_f$.

nodes.name: Reduction of $E$ modulo $\G$
nodes.statement: For any smooth hypersurface (smooth irreducible codimension-one subvariety) $\G$ in $\PP^n$, the local ring at $\G$ is a discrete valuation ring $\Ocal_\G$ with maximal ideal $\frak{m}_\G$. We denote the reduction map $\Ocal_\G \longrightarrow \Ocal_\G/\frak{m}_\G= \CQ(\G)$ by $f \longmapsto f_\G$. Then for $\G \neq H_\infty$, the reduction of $E$ modulo $\G$, $E_\G$ is the cubic curve (possibly singular) over $\CQ(\G)$ defined by $$Y^2Z=X^3+A_\G XZ^2+B_\G Z^3,$$ as $A,B \in \Ocal_\G$ for all $\G \neq H_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Reducing the Weierstrass coefficients through the DVR $\Ocal_\G$ gives the (possibly singular) cubic $E_\G$ over $\CQ(\G)$.

nodes.name: Non-singular points $E_\G(\CQ(\G))_{\text{ns}}$ and the subgroup $E_0(K)$
nodes.statement: Let $$E_\G(\CQ(\G))_{\text{ns}}:=\{ \text{ non-singular points of }E_\G(\CQ(\G))\} $$ and $$E_0(K)=\{ P \in E(K) \ | \ P_\G \in E_\G(\CQ(\G))_{\text{ns}}\}, $$

nodes.name: The $K$-isomorphic curve $E'/K$ with no pole at $H_\infty$
nodes.statement: Let $k:=\max\left\{ \left\lceil \frac{\deg A}{4}\right\rceil, \left\lceil \frac{\deg B}{6}\right\rceil \right\}$ and \begin{equation} E'/K: \qquad Y^2Z=X^3+\left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{4k}AXZ^2+\left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{6k}BZ^3, \end{equation} which is the elliptic curve obtained from $E/K$ by the group isomorphism \begin{align*} E/K &\stackrel{\approx}{\longrightarrow} E'/K \\ P=[x:y:z] &\longmapsto P'=[x':y':z']:=\left[\left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{2k}x: \left(\frac{S_0}{S_1}\right)^{3k}y:z \right]. \end{align*} The choice of $k$ is to make sure the Weierstrass equation $(\ref{WE'})$ is still minimal with respect to all prime divisors except at the hyperplane $H'_\infty$ defined by $S_1=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Change of variables scaling $A$ and $B$ by $(S_0/S_1)^{4k}$ and $(S_0/S_1)^{6k}$ to move the bad hyperplane from $H_\infty$ to $H'_\infty$.

nodes.name: The finite set $B_P$ of codimension-two subvarieties
nodes.statement: if we let $$B_P:=\left\{ H_\infty\cap H'_\infty, \ \text{dimension-$(n-2)$ components of }I_{f_P}\cup I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_P\cup S_{P'} \right\}, $$

nodes.name: The singular specialization locus $S_P$
nodes.statement: if we let $S_P$ be the set of all $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H_\infty(\CQ)$ such that the specialized point $P_t$ is a singular point on the specialized fiber $E_t$
differentia: the specialized point $P_t$ is a singular point on the specialized fiber $E_t$

nodes.name: Canonical height pairing on $E(K)$
nodes.statement: The canonical height pairing on $E(K)$ is $$\< \cdot , \cdot \>_E : E(K) \times E(K) \longrightarrow \RR $$ $$\<P, Q\>_E \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E}(P+Q)-\hat{h}_{E}(P)-\hat{h}_{E}(Q) \right).$$
nodes.origin_citation: Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapter 6

nodes.name: Canonical height pairing on $E_\G(\CQ(\G))$
nodes.statement: Likewise, for any smooth hypersurface $\G \subset \PP^n$ such that $E_\G$ is non-singular, the canonical height pairing on $E_{\G}(\CQ(\G))$ is $$\< \cdot , \cdot \>_{E_{\G}} : E_{\G}(\CQ(\G)) \times E_{\G}(\CQ(\G)) \longrightarrow \RR $$ $$\<P_{\G}, Q_{\G}\>_{E_{\G}} \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E_{\G}}(P_{\G}+Q_{\G})-\hat{h}_{E_{\G}}(P_{\G})-\hat{h}_{E_{\G}}(Q_{\G}) \right).$$
nodes.origin_citation: Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapter 6

nodes.name: Specialization map $\s_t$
nodes.statement: One can view $E/K$ as the generic fiber of an abelian scheme $\pi : \Ecal \longrightarrow U$, for some Zariski open dense subset $U \subset \PP^n$. Then for all $t \in U(\CQ)$, the specialization map \begin{align*} \s_t : E(K) &\longrightarrow E_t(\CQ) \\ P &\longmapsto P_t \end{align*} is a group homomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: For $t$ in the open set $U$ over which $\Ecal \to U$ is an abelian scheme, $\s_t$ sends $P \in E(K)$ to its fiber value $P_t$.

nodes.name: Normalized Weil height $h_C$ on a curve
nodes.statement: There is a Weil height $h_{C,\phi}$ (that depends on the closed embedding of $\phi : C \longhookrightarrow \PP^m$) on $C(\CQ)$ and we normalize it to $h_C:=h_{C,\phi}/\deg \phi$.

nodes.name: Homogeneous coordinates, the function field $K=\CQ(\PP^n)$ and the infinity hyperplane $H_\infty$
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 2$ and $S_0, \ldots, S_n$ be the homogeneous coordinate functions of the projective space $\PP^n$ over $\CQ$. Let $K=\CQ(\PP^n)$ be the function field of $\PP^n$. If we denote $T_1:=\frac{S_1}{S_0}, \ldots, T_n:=\frac{S_n}{S_0}$, then $K=\CQ(T_1, \ldots, T_n)$ and the infinity hyperplane $H_\infty$ is the plane defined by $S_0=0$

nodes.name: Minimality of the Weierstrass equation away from $H_\infty$
nodes.statement: with $A,B \in \CQ[T_1, \ldots, T_n]$ such that it is minimal with respect to all prime divisors in $\PP^n$ that are not $H_\infty$, i.e. $$0\leq \ord_D(A) <4 \qquad \text{or}\qquad 0\leq \ord_D(B)<6 $$ for all prime divisors $D \neq H_\infty$. Such a Weierstrass equation can always be obtained via change of variables.
nodes.statement_short: The defining Weierstrass equation is assumed minimal at every prime divisor other than $H_\infty$.

nodes.name: Standing setting for the lemmas of Section 3
nodes.statement: All the lemmas in this section are based on the setting mentioned above.

nodes.name: Weierstrass equation defining $E/K$

nodes.name: Discriminant $\D_E$ of $E$
nodes.statement: The discriminant $$\D_E=-16(4A^3+27B^2) $$ is a non-zero element in $\CQ[T_1, \ldots, T_n]$.

nodes.name: Convergence of the average of $\hat{h}_{E_t}(P_t)/h_{\PP^n}(t)$
nodes.statement: Even in this simple case of $\PP^n$ with $n\geq 2$, it is still an open question whether this average converges, let alone whether it converges to $\hat{h}_{E}(P)$.

nodes.name: Prior work on fibers over points of $\PP^n$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, instead of looking at the fibers over smooth hypersurfaces of $\PP^n$, the author (\cite{WWP}) also tried to generalize Silverman's theorem by looking at the fibers over points of $\PP^n$ of $E/\QQ(\PP^n)$. As remarked in that paper, the limit of the quotient $\hat{h}_{E_{t}}(P_t)/h_{\PP^n}(t) $ doesn't exist when $h_{\PP^n}(t)$ tends to infinity for $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)$. Thus, the author studied instead the average value of the quotient $\hat{h}_{E_{t}}(P_t)/h_{\PP^n}(t)$ over rational $t \in \PP^n(\QQ)$ with bounded height. As the bound tends to infinity, the author showed that this average remains finite and uniformly bounded below by a nonzero constant for all non-torsion $P$ in $E(\QQ(\PP^n))$.
nodes.statement_short: In the author's earlier paper the pointwise quotient has no limit, but its average over bounded-height rational $t$ stays finite and bounded below.

nodes.name: Comparison of Theorem A with the elliptic surface version of Silverman's theorem
nodes.statement: Our Theorem A is analogous to the elliptic surface version of Silverman's theorem despite the fact that there's no limit involved and we view $\deg \G$ as the Weil height of $\G$. The main reason for this difference is the type of global field over which the reduction $E_\G$ is defined: over a curve $C$, $\G=\{t\}$ is a point and $E_t$ is an elliptic curve over a number field, whereas over $\PP^n$ for $n \geq 2$, $E_{\G}$ is an elliptic curve over a function field. Consequently, the canonical height $\hat{h}_{E_{t}}$ on $E_{t}(\CQ)$ is derived from a Weil height in a number field and the canonical height $\hat{h}_{E_{\G}}$ on $E_{\G}(\CQ(\G))$ is derived from a Weil height in a function field. As we shall see in section \ref{lemma}, the theory of Weil heights over the function field of a smooth hypersurface is related to the intersection theory of divisors in the projective space, i.e. B\'ezout's theorem and this is where the degree of $\G$ comes into play.
nodes.statement_short: No limit is needed because over $\PP^n$ with $n \geq 2$ the fiber $E_\G$ lives over a function field, so $\deg \G$ plays the role of the Weil height via B\u00e9zout.

nodes.name: Outline of the paper and proof strategy
nodes.statement: In section \ref{HF}, we remind the readers of the definition of the Weil height and canonical height on an elliptic curve defined over $k(V)$, the function field of an arbitrary smooth projective variety $V$ defined over a number field $k$. From now onwards, we will use the convention that varieties and subvarieties are always irreducible. Next, in section \ref{lemma}, we will prove some lemmas that relate the Weil heights on $E(K)$ and $E_\G(\CQ(\G))$. In fact, the first few lemmas show that the equality in Theorem A holds for Weil heights on $E_\G$, for a hypersurface $\G$ that does not contain certain codimension-two subvarieties in $\PP^n$ that depend on $P$. To pass from Weil heights to canonical heights, we will replace $P$ by $[2^m]P$, divide the Weil heights by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and take the limit $m \rightarrow \infty$. The rest of the lemmas are used to show that the dependence of $\G$ on infinitely many $[2^m]P$ can be reduced to just not containing a finite number of codimension-two subvarieties. In the last section, we will apply Theorem A to prove Theorem B.
nodes.statement_short: Roadmap: recall heights, prove Weil-height lemmas, pass to canonical heights by replacing $P$ with $[2^m]P$ and dividing by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$, then deduce Theorem B.

nodes.name: Why induced rational maps control the Weil height
nodes.statement: As we have seen from the previous section, the Weil height $h_E(P)$ of a point $P\in E(\overline{k}(V))$ is directly related to the rational map induced by $P$. So in order to study the relationship between $h_{E}(P)$ and $h_{E_\G}(P_\G)$, we look at the corresponding induced rational maps.

nodes.name: Passage from Weil heights to canonical heights via $[2^m]P$
nodes.statement: In order to obtain Theorem A from Lemma \ref{leh}, we will replace $P$ in equation (\ref{E1}) by $[2^m]P$, then divide the resulting equation by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and take the limit $m\rightarrow \infty$. This leads us to study the indeterminacy locus of $f_{[2^m]P}$ when $m$ goes to infinity.

nodes.statement: So far, the lemmas above allow us to control the indeterminacy of $f_{[2^m]P}$ over $\PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H_\infty$. Since $H_\infty$ is the pole of $A$ and $B$, the reduction mod $H_\infty$ of $E$ is not defined. To overcome this, we use the following change of variables in $K$ to obtain an elliptic curve $E'$ that is $K$-isomorphic to $E$, defined by a Weierstrass equation whose coefficients don't have pole at $H_\infty$:

nodes.name: Reduction to codimension-two singular specialization locus
nodes.statement: The next lemma allows us to reduce to the case where the points $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)$ for which $P_t$ is a singular point on $E_t$ are of codimension at least $2$ in $\PP^n(\CQ)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is a rational map between smooth projective varieties, the indeterminacy locus $I_f$ has codimension at least $2$, i.e. each irreducible component of $I_f$ has dimension at most $n-2$. Define the quasi-projective varieties $U^o:=\PP^n\backslash I_f$ and $\G^o:=\G\backslash I_f \cap \G$ and we have the following commutative diagram $$\xymatrix{ \G^o \ar@{^{(}->}[d]_{j_{\G^o}} \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{\iota_{\G^o}} &U^o \ar@{->}[r]^{f|_{U^o}} \ar@{^{(}->}[d]_{j_{U^o}} &\PP^r \\ \G \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{\iota_\G} &\PP^n \ar@{-->}[ur]_f} $$ where all the $\iota$ and $j$ are inclusion maps and $f|_{U^o}$ is the restriction of $f$ on $U^o$. Since $\G$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_f$, the codimension of $I_f \cap \G$ in $\G$ is at least $2$ also. Thus, we have the following isomorphisms of divisor class groups induced by $j_{\G^o}$ and $j_{U^o}$: \begin{align*} j^*_{U^o}: \Pic(\PP^n) &\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \Pic(U^o) &j^*_{\G^o}: \Pic(\G) &\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \Pic(\G^o)\\ c &\longmapsto c \cap U^o & D &\longmapsto D \cap \G^o, \end{align*} with projective closure in the corresponding varieties as the inverse maps. With these isomorphisms and the above commutative diagram, we obtain the following commutative diagram of divisor class groups: $$\xymatrix{ \Pic(\G^o) &\Pic(U^o) \ar@{->}[l]_{\iota_{\G^o}^*} &\Pic(\PP^r) \ar@{->}[l]_{f|_{U^o}^*} \ar@{->}[dl]^{f^{-1}} \\ \Pic(\G) \ar@{->}[u]^{j_{\G^o}^*}_\cong &\Pic(\PP^n) \ar@{->}[u]^{j_{U^o}^*}_\cong \ar@{->}[l]_{\iota_\G^*} }$$ Pull-backs are functorial on the category of varieties (\cite{FIT} Chapter 2, Section 2.2, \cite{HAG} Appendix A, Theorem 1.1), so for any divisor class $c \in \Pic(\PP^r)$, we have $$\iota_{\G^o}^*(f|_{U^o}^*(c))=(f|_{U^o} \circ \iota_{\G^o})^*(c). $$ Then by taking $(j_{\G^o}^*)^{-1}$, the projective closure in $\G$ and tracing the commutative diagram, we get \begin{align*} \iota_{\G}^*(f^{-1}(c))&=(j_{\G^o}^*)^{-1}\left(\iota_{\G^o}^*(f|_{U^o}^*(c))\right) \\& = (j_{\G^o}^*)^{-1}\left((f|_{U^o} \circ \iota_{\G^o})^*(c)\right) \\ &= (f \circ \iota_\G)^{-1}(c), \end{align*} which is the statement of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the complement of $I_f$, use the $\Pic$ isomorphisms induced by the two inclusions, and chase the commutative diagram using functoriality of pull-backs.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: Let $g_{P_\G} : \G \dashrightarrow \PP^2$ be the rational map induced by $P_\G=[x_\G: y_\G: z_\G]$. Then $g_{P_\G}$ factors through $$\xymatrix{ \G \ar@{-->}[r]^{g_{P_\G}} \ar@{^{(}->}[d]_{\iota_{\G}} &\PP^2 \\ \PP^n \ar@{-->}[ur]_{f_P} }$$ Let $L \in \Pic(\PP^2)$ be the divisor class of hyperplanes, then we have \begin{align*} h_{E_\G}(P_\G)&= \deg g_{P_\G}^{-1}(L) & (\text{by Proposition \ref{LH}})\\ &=\deg (f_P \circ \iota_\G)^{-1}(L)\\ &= \deg \iota_\G^* (f_P^{-1}(L)) &(\text{by Lemma \ref{Le1}}). \end{align*} But the divisor class $\iota_\G^* (f_P^{-1}(L))$ is the divisor class of the intersection of $\G$ and $f_P^{-1}(L)$ (\cite{FIT} Chapter 8, Example 8.1.7 or \cite{HAG} Chapter II, Exercises 6.2). Then by B\'ezout's theorem, we get $\deg \iota_\G^* (f_P^{-1}(L)) = \deg \G \cdot \deg f_P^{-1}(L)$, which gives $$h_{E_\G}(P_\G)=\deg \G \cdot \deg f_P^{-1}(L)=\deg \G \cdot h_E(P) $$ by Proposition \ref{LH} again.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $h_{E_\G}(P_\G)$ as a pull-back degree via Lang's proposition, rewrite it with Lemma 2, then apply B\u00e9zout's theorem to factor out $\deg \G$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: For any smooth hypersurface $\G$, its local ring $\Ocal_\G$ is a DVR with fraction field $K$ and residue field $\CQ(\G)$, which is a perfect field. With the minimality assumption on the Weierstrass equation, $E/K$ is defined by a Weierstrass equation with coefficients in $\Ocal_\G$ and minimal with respect to the prime divisor $\G$. Thus, the smooth part of the Weierstrass model gives the N\'eron model of $E/K$ and the quotient group $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite (\cite{SAT} Chapter IV, Corollary 9.2d). So there exists $n_\G \in \NN$ such that $([n_\G]P)_\G$ is not a singular point on $E_\G(\CQ(\G))$. Since $E_\G/\CQ(\G)$ is singular if and only if $\G$ is a component of the discriminant locus and there are only finitely many such components $\G_1, \ldots, \G_\ell$. So $N:=\lcm\{n_{\G_1}, \dots, n_{\G_\ell}\}$ will satisfy the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality makes the smooth Weierstrass model the N\u00e9ron model, so $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite; take the lcm of the finitely many local exponents.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: If we write $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$ where the homogeneous polynomials $x,y,z \in \CQ[S_0, \ldots, S_n]$ have no common irreducible factor, then the induced rational map $f_P$ is not defined at $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)$ if and only if $x(t)=y(t)=z(t)=0$, because $f_P$ maps from $\PP^n$ and so there's no way to alter it. The corresponding point $P'$ is $[S_0^{2k}S_1^kx: S_0^{3k}y: S_1^{3k}z]$. Since at least one of $x,y,z$ has no $S_0$ as its factor, we consider all possible cases: Case 1: $z$ doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. Then the only possible irreducible common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx$, $S_0^{3k}y$, $S_1^{3k}z$ is $S_1$ and even if we factor out this common factor, the induced rational map $f_{P'}$ is still not defined at $t=[0:1:*:\ldots:*]$. Case 2: $y$ doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. In this case, the only possible common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx, S_0^{3k}y, S_1^{3k}z$ are $S_1$ and $S_0$. After removing the common factors, let $P'=[x'':y'':z'']$. Since $y(t)=0$ and the only possible factor we factor away from $y$ in $ S_0^{3k}y$ is $S_1$, thus $y''(t)=0$. Also, $t=[0:1:*:\ldots:*] \in H_\infty(\CQ) \backslash H'_\infty(\CQ)$ by assumption. If $P'_t$ is well-defined, then it is a point on the cubic curve $E_t'(\CQ)$ with zero $Y$-coordinate, which implies $P'_t$ is either a singular point or a torsion point of order $2$ on $E'_t(\CQ)$. Case 3: $x$ doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. The highest power of $S_0$ that can be a common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx, S_0^{3k}y, S_1^{3k}z$ is $S_0^{2k}$. After removing the common factors, let $P'=[x'':y'':z'']$, then we see that $y''$ always has $S_0^k$ as a factor. Thus $y''(t)=0$ and the argument follows as Case 2.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on which of $x,y,z$ is not divisible by $S_0$, tracking the common factors removed from $P'$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A
nodes.statement:
Now, we put ourselves in the setting described in Section ef{lemma}. From Lemma ef{leh}, if $\G$ is a smooth hypersurface that does not contain any codimension-two component of the indeterminacy locus of $f_{[2^m]P}$ for infinitely many $m$, then equality (ef{E1}) holds for these $[2^m]P$ and thus dividing equation (ef{E1}) by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and then taking the limit $mightarrow \infty$ over all $m$ such that equality (ef{E1}) holds will give us the equality in Theorem A. A priori, such $\G$ might have to avoid containing infinitely many codimension-two subvarieties in $\PP^n$ corresponding to the infinitely many rational maps $f_{[2^m]P}$, we will prove that this is not a problem. In fact, we will prove that besides finitely many codimension-two subvarieties in $\PP^n$ that might be common components of the indeterminacy locus of all $f_{[2^m]P}$, $m \in \NN$, other codimension-two components of the indeterminacy locus of a particular $f_{[2^m]P}$ will never reappear as components of the indeterminacy locus of $f_{[2^\ell]P}$ for any $\ell > m$. Since the canonical height is a quadratic form, we may replace $P$ by $[N]P$ in Theorem A. Given any $P \in E(K)$, we replace $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $ef{LNS}$ to assure that $P_\G$ is not a singular point of $E_\G$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\G 
eq H_\infty$. So if we let $S_P$ be the set of all $t \in \PP^n(\CQ) ackslash H_\infty(\CQ)$ such that the specialized point $P_t$ is a singular point on the specialized fiber $E_t$, then $S_P$ is an algebraic set (since singularity is an algebraic property) of codimension at least two in $\PP^n ackslash H_\infty$. In addition, we note that $S_P$ is contained in the discriminant locus $\D_E=0$. Similarly, we may assume the same for the corresponding point $P'$ on the isomorphic curve $E'$ defined by equation $(ef{WE'})$, i.e. $P'_\G$ is not a singular point of $E'_\G$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\G 
eq H'_\infty$ and $S_{P'}$ has codimension at least $2$ in $\PP^n(\CQ) ackslash H'_\infty(\CQ)$. As before, let $I_{f_P}$ be the indeterminacy locus of the rational map $f_P$ induced by $P$. Then for all $t \in \PP^n(\CQ) ackslash H_\infty(\CQ)$ that are not in $I_{f_P} \cup S_P$, $f_P(t)=P_t$ is well-defined and is not a singular point on the cubic curve $E_t$. By lemma ef{DL} and induction on $m$, $f_{[2^m]P}(t)=\left( [2^m]Pight)_t=[2^m]P_t$ is well-defined for all $m \in \NN$. Thus, $$I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap \left(\PP^n(\CQ) ackslash H_\infty(\CQ) ight) \subset I_{f_P}\cup S_P, \qquad	ext{ for all }m \in \NN.$$ The exact same argument works for $P'$ and so we also have $$I_{f_{[2^m]P'}} \cap \left(\PP^n(\CQ) ackslash H'_\infty(\CQ) ight) \subset I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_{P'}\qquad	ext{ for all } m \in \NN.$$ For $$t=[0:1:*: \dots:*] \in \left(I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\CQ)ight)  ackslash H'_\infty(\CQ),$$ if $t 
ot \in I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_{P'}$, then lemma ef{DL} says that $f_{[2^m]P'}(t)=([2^m]P')_t$ is defined and non-singular on $E'_t$ because $([2^m]P')_t=[2^m]P'_t$. In particular, lemma ef{PL} implies that in fact $[2^m]P'$ is a point of order $2$ on $E'_t$. Thus, for $\ell > m$, $([2^\ell]P')_t=[2^\ell]P'_t=[2^{\ell-m}]\left([2^m]P'_tight)=O_{E'_t}$, which implies that $t$ is not in $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ by the contrapositive statement of lemma ef{PL}. Notice that we are left with $t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\CQ)\cap H'_\infty(\CQ)$, which is an algebraic set of codimension at least $2$ in $\PP^n(\CQ)$. To summarize, we have shown that given $P\in E(K)$, by replacing $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $ef{LNS}$ if necessary, so that $P_\G$ and $P'_\G$ are not singular points of $E_\G$ and $E'_\G$ respectively for all smooth hypersurface $\G$, for any $m \in \NN$, if $$ t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \quad	ext{and}\quad t 
otin I_{f_P} \cup I_{f_{P'}} \cup S_P \cup S_{P'} \cup (H_\infty(\CQ)\cap H'_\infty(\CQ)), $$ then for any $\ell>m$, $t 
ot \in I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$. In particular, if we let $$B_P:=\left\{ H_\infty\cap H'_\infty, \ 	ext{dimension-$(n-2)$ components of }I_{f_P}\cup I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_P\cup S_{P'} ight\}, $$then for any $m \in \NN$, if $C$ is a dimension-$(n-2)$ component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ that is not in $B_P$, then $C$ is not a component of $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ for all $\ell > m$. To complete the proof for Theorem A, we consider any smooth hypersurface $\G \subset \PP^n$ that is not a component of the discriminant locus, so $E_\G$ is an elliptic curve over $\CQ(\G)$. Furthermore, if $\G$ does not contain any subvariety in $B_P$, then we have just shown that $\G$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ for all big enough $m \in \NN$. So by lemma ef{leh}, we have $$ rac{h_{E_\G}([2^m]P_\G)}{\deg \G}= rac{h_{E_\G}(\left([2^m]Pight)_\G)}{\deg \G}= h_E([2^m]P) $$ for all big enough $m \in \NN$. Dividing this equation by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and then taking the limit $mightarrow \infty$ will give us Theorem A.
nodes.statement_short: Show that new codimension-two components of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ never recur for larger $m$, so a hypersurface avoiding the finite set $B_P$ satisfies Lemma 3 for all large $m$; divide by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and let $m \to \infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Split on whether the $K/\CQ$-trace vanishes; in the zero-trace case use positive definiteness of the height pairing plus Theorem A to keep the Gram determinant non-zero, reduce the dimension by hyperplane sections, and induct on $n$ for Zariski density.

nodes.name: Codimension of the indeterminacy locus
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is a rational map between smooth projective varieties, the indeterminacy locus $I_f$ has codimension at least $2$, i.e. each irreducible component of $I_f$ has dimension at most $n-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Record that each component of $I_f$ has dimension at most $n-2$.

nodes.name: Definition of $U^o$, $\G^o$ and the commutative diagram
nodes.statement: Define the quasi-projective varieties $U^o:=\PP^n\backslash I_f$ and $\G^o:=\G\backslash I_f \cap \G$ and we have the following commutative diagram $$\xymatrix{ \G^o \ar@{^{(}->}[d]_{j_{\G^o}} \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{\iota_{\G^o}} &U^o \ar@{->}[r]^{f|_{U^o}} \ar@{^{(}->}[d]_{j_{U^o}} &\PP^r \\ \G \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^{\iota_\G} &\PP^n \ar@{-->}[ur]_f} $$ where all the $\iota$ and $j$ are inclusion maps and $f|_{U^o}$ is the restriction of $f$ on $U^o$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the loci where $f$ is defined and the corresponding inclusion diagram.

nodes.name: Isomorphisms of divisor class groups
nodes.statement: Since $\G$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_f$, the codimension of $I_f \cap \G$ in $\G$ is at least $2$ also. Thus, we have the following isomorphisms of divisor class groups induced by $j_{\G^o}$ and $j_{U^o}$: \begin{align*} j^*_{U^o}: \Pic(\PP^n) &\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \Pic(U^o) &j^*_{\G^o}: \Pic(\G) &\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \Pic(\G^o)\\ c &\longmapsto c \cap U^o & D &\longmapsto D \cap \G^o, \end{align*} with projective closure in the corresponding varieties as the inverse maps.
nodes.statement_short: Since $I_f \cap \G$ has codimension $\geq 2$ in $\G$, restriction gives $\Pic$ isomorphisms for both $\PP^n$ and $\G$.

nodes.name: Functoriality of pull-backs
nodes.statement: With these isomorphisms and the above commutative diagram, we obtain the following commutative diagram of divisor class groups: $$\xymatrix{ \Pic(\G^o) &\Pic(U^o) \ar@{->}[l]_{\iota_{\G^o}^*} &\Pic(\PP^r) \ar@{->}[l]_{f|_{U^o}^*} \ar@{->}[dl]^{f^{-1}} \\ \Pic(\G) \ar@{->}[u]^{j_{\G^o}^*}_\cong &\Pic(\PP^n) \ar@{->}[u]^{j_{U^o}^*}_\cong \ar@{->}[l]_{\iota_\G^*} }$$ Pull-backs are functorial on the category of varieties (\cite{FIT} Chapter 2, Section 2.2, \cite{HAG} Appendix A, Theorem 1.1), so for any divisor class $c \in \Pic(\PP^r)$, we have $$\iota_{\G^o}^*(f|_{U^o}^*(c))=(f|_{U^o} \circ \iota_{\G^o})^*(c). $$
nodes.statement_short: Apply functoriality of pull-backs on the diagram of divisor class groups.

nodes.name: Conclusion by taking projective closure in $\G$
nodes.statement: Then by taking $(j_{\G^o}^*)^{-1}$, the projective closure in $\G$ and tracing the commutative diagram, we get \begin{align*} \iota_{\G}^*(f^{-1}(c))&=(j_{\G^o}^*)^{-1}\left(\iota_{\G^o}^*(f|_{U^o}^*(c))\right) \\& = (j_{\G^o}^*)^{-1}\left((f|_{U^o} \circ \iota_{\G^o})^*(c)\right) \\ &= (f \circ \iota_\G)^{-1}(c), \end{align*} which is the statement of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Invert $j_{\G^o}^*$ and trace the diagram to obtain the claimed equality.

nodes.name: The rational map induced by $P_\G$ factors through $\G$
nodes.statement: Let $g_{P_\G} : \G \dashrightarrow \PP^2$ be the rational map induced by $P_\G=[x_\G: y_\G: z_\G]$. Then $g_{P_\G}$ factors through
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $g_{P_\G}$ and note it factors as $f_P \circ \iota_\G$.

nodes.name: Rewrite $h_{E_\G}(P_\G)$ as a pull-back degree
nodes.statement: Let $L \in \Pic(\PP^2)$ be the divisor class of hyperplanes, then we have \begin{align*} h_{E_\G}(P_\G)&= \deg g_{P_\G}^{-1}(L) & (\text{by Proposition \ref{LH}})\\ &=\deg (f_P \circ \iota_\G)^{-1}(L)\\ &= \deg \iota_\G^* (f_P^{-1}(L)) &(\text{by Lemma \ref{Le1}}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use Lang's proposition and Lemma 2 to write $h_{E_\G}(P_\G)=\deg \iota_\G^*(f_P^{-1}(L))$.

nodes.name: Identify the restricted class with an intersection class
nodes.statement: But the divisor class $\iota_\G^* (f_P^{-1}(L))$ is the divisor class of the intersection of $\G$ and $f_P^{-1}(L)$ (\cite{FIT} Chapter 8, Example 8.1.7 or \cite{HAG} Chapter II, Exercises 6.2).
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\iota_\G^*(f_P^{-1}(L))$ with the intersection class of $\G$ and $f_P^{-1}(L)$.

nodes.name: Apply Bézout's theorem and conclude
nodes.statement: Then by B\'ezout's theorem, we get $\deg \iota_\G^* (f_P^{-1}(L)) = \deg \G \cdot \deg f_P^{-1}(L)$, which gives $$h_{E_\G}(P_\G)=\deg \G \cdot \deg f_P^{-1}(L)=\deg \G \cdot h_E(P) $$ by Proposition \ref{LH} again.
nodes.statement_short: B\u00e9zout's theorem factors out $\deg \G$, giving $h_{E_\G}(P_\G)=\deg \G \cdot h_E(P)$.

nodes.statement:
For $E/K$ defined by the Weierstrass equation $(ef{WE})$ with $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$ where $x,y,z \in \CQ[S_0,\ldots,S_n]$, the doubling formula (\cite{SAT} Chapter IV, page 324) is  egin{align}&[2]P=
otag \* &[2yz\left(\left(3x^2+Az^2ight)^2-2xz(2y)^2ight): 
otag \ &-\left(3x^2+Az^2ight)^3+z(2y)^2\left(8x^3+2Axz^2-Bz^3-y^2zight): 
otag \ &8y^3z^3]. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Write down the classical doubling formula for $P=[x:y:z]$.

nodes.name: Second form of the doubling formula
nodes.statement:
By substituting the relation $x^3=y^2z-Axz^2-Bz^3$ into the first two coordinates and then factor away the common factor $z^2$, we also have  egin{align}&[2]P=
otag \ &[2y\left(xy^2-3Ax^2z-9Bxz^2+A^2z^3ight): 
otag \ &4y^2\left(7y^2-6Axz-9Bz^2ight)-\left(27(y^2-Axz-Bz^2)^2+27Ax^4+9A^2x^2z^2+A^3z^4ight): 
otag \ &8y^3z]. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $x^3=y^2z-Axz^2-Bz^3$ and cancel $z^2$ to get an alternative formula.

nodes.name: $y(t)$ and $z(t)$ cannot both vanish
nodes.statement: Since by assumption $t\in\PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H_\infty$ such that $P_t=f_P(t)=[x(t):y(t):z(t)]$ is defined and is a non-singular point on the cubic curve $E_t$, so $y(t)$ and $z(t)$ cannot be both zero. It is clear that $f_{[2]P}$ is defined when both $y(t)$ and $z(t)$ are not zero.
nodes.statement_short: Non-singularity of $P_t$ forces $y(t),z(t)$ not both zero, which settles the generic case.

nodes.name: Case $y(t)=0$
nodes.statement: When $y(t)=0$, then $3x(t)^2+A(t)z(t)^2$ is not zero or otherwise $P_t$ is a singular point on $E_t$. So formula $(\ref{D1})$ gives $([2]P)_t=[0:1:0]$, which is not a surprise as $P_t=[x(t):0:z(t)]$ is always a 2-torsion point with the given Weierstrass equation (\ref{WEt}).
nodes.statement_short: If $y(t)=0$ the first formula gives $([2]P)_t=[0:1:0]$, consistent with $P_t$ being $2$-torsion.

nodes.name: Case $z(t)=0$
nodes.statement: When $z(t)=0$, then $x(t)=0$ and $y(t) \neq 0$, since $P_t$ is a point on $E_t$. Formula $(\ref{D2})$ gives $([2]P)_t=[0:y(t)^4:0]=[0:1:0]$. Thus the induced rational map $f_{[2]P}$ is defined at such $t$.
nodes.statement_short: If $z(t)=0$ the second formula gives $([2]P)_t=[0:1:0]$, so $f_{[2]P}$ is defined at $t$.

nodes.name: Compatibility of the two formulae
nodes.statement: Lastly, formulae $(\ref{D1})$ and $(\ref{D2})$ are the same (with $A,B$ replaced by $A(t)$ and $B(t)$) doubling formula on the cubic curve $E_t$, so $([2]P)_t=[2]P_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Both formulae specialize to the doubling formula on $E_t$, hence $([2]P)_t=[2]P_t$.

nodes.name: The local ring at $\G$ is a DVR with perfect residue field
nodes.statement: For any smooth hypersurface $\G$, its local ring $\Ocal_\G$ is a DVR with fraction field $K$ and residue field $\CQ(\G)$, which is a perfect field.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the DVR $\Ocal_\G$ with fraction field $K$ and perfect residue field $\CQ(\G)$.

nodes.name: Minimality gives the Néron model and finiteness of $E(K)/E_0(K)$
nodes.statement: With the minimality assumption on the Weierstrass equation, $E/K$ is defined by a Weierstrass equation with coefficients in $\Ocal_\G$ and minimal with respect to the prime divisor $\G$. Thus, the smooth part of the Weierstrass model gives the N\'eron model of $E/K$ and the quotient group $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite (\cite{SAT} Chapter IV, Corollary 9.2d).
nodes.statement_short: Minimality identifies the smooth Weierstrass model with the N\u00e9ron model, so $E(K)/E_0(K)$ is finite.

nodes.name: Existence of a local exponent $n_\G$
nodes.statement: So there exists $n_\G \in \NN$ such that $([n_\G]P)_\G$ is not a singular point on $E_\G(\CQ(\G))$.
nodes.statement_short: Extract for each $\G$ an integer $n_\G$ making $([n_\G]P)_\G$ non-singular.

nodes.name: Take the lcm over the finitely many bad hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: Since $E_\G/\CQ(\G)$ is singular if and only if $\G$ is a component of the discriminant locus and there are only finitely many such components $\G_1, \ldots, \G_\ell$. So $N:=\lcm\{n_{\G_1}, \dots, n_{\G_\ell}\}$ will satisfy the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Only components of the discriminant locus are bad, so $N=\lcm\{n_{\G_i}\}$ works.

nodes.name: Undefined points of $f_P$ and the coordinates of $P'$
nodes.statement: If we write $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$ where the homogeneous polynomials $x,y,z \in \CQ[S_0, \ldots, S_n]$ have no common irreducible factor, then the induced rational map $f_P$ is not defined at $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)$ if and only if $x(t)=y(t)=z(t)=0$, because $f_P$ maps from $\PP^n$ and so there's no way to alter it. The corresponding point $P'$ is $[S_0^{2k}S_1^kx: S_0^{3k}y: S_1^{3k}z]$. Since at least one of $x,y,z$ has no $S_0$ as its factor, we consider all possible cases:
nodes.statement_short: $f_P$ is undefined at $t$ exactly when all three coordinates vanish; write out $P'$ and split on which coordinate lacks the factor $S_0$.

nodes.name: Case 1: $z$ has no factor $S_0$
nodes.statement: Case 1: $z$ doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. Then the only possible irreducible common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx$, $S_0^{3k}y$, $S_1^{3k}z$ is $S_1$ and even if we factor out this common factor, the induced rational map $f_{P'}$ is still not defined at $t=[0:1:*:\ldots:*]$.
nodes.statement_short: Only $S_1$ can be cancelled, so $f_{P'}$ is still undefined at $t$ (alternative a).

nodes.name: Case 2: $y$ has no factor $S_0$
nodes.statement: Case 2: $y$ doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. In this case, the only possible common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx, S_0^{3k}y, S_1^{3k}z$ are $S_1$ and $S_0$. After removing the common factors, let $P'=[x'':y'':z'']$. Since $y(t)=0$ and the only possible factor we factor away from $y$ in $ S_0^{3k}y$ is $S_1$, thus $y''(t)=0$. Also, $t=[0:1:*:\ldots:*] \in H_\infty(\CQ) \backslash H'_\infty(\CQ)$ by assumption. If $P'_t$ is well-defined, then it is a point on the cubic curve $E_t'(\CQ)$ with zero $Y$-coordinate, which implies $P'_t$ is either a singular point or a torsion point of order $2$ on $E'_t(\CQ)$.
nodes.statement_short: Here $y''(t)=0$, so $P'_t$ is either singular or of order $2$ (alternatives b, c).

nodes.name: Case 3: $x$ has no factor $S_0$
nodes.statement: Case 3: $x$ doesn't have $S_0$ as its factor. The highest power of $S_0$ that can be a common factor of the homogeneous polynomials $S_0^{2k}S_1^kx, S_0^{3k}y, S_1^{3k}z$ is $S_0^{2k}$. After removing the common factors, let $P'=[x'':y'':z'']$, then we see that $y''$ always has $S_0^k$ as a factor. Thus $y''(t)=0$ and the argument follows as Case 2.
nodes.statement_short: $y''$ still carries the factor $S_0^k$, so Case 2's argument applies.

nodes.name: Strategy: control the codimension-two components of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$
nodes.statement: Now, we put ourselves in the setting described in Section \ref{lemma}. From Lemma \ref{leh}, if $\G$ is a smooth hypersurface that does not contain any codimension-two component of the indeterminacy locus of $f_{[2^m]P}$ for infinitely many $m$, then equality (\ref{E1}) holds for these $[2^m]P$ and thus dividing equation (\ref{E1}) by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and then taking the limit $m\rightarrow \infty$ over all $m$ such that equality (\ref{E1}) holds will give us the equality in Theorem A. A priori, such $\G$ might have to avoid containing infinitely many codimension-two subvarieties in $\PP^n$ corresponding to the infinitely many rational maps $f_{[2^m]P}$, we will prove that this is not a problem. In fact, we will prove that besides finitely many codimension-two subvarieties in $\PP^n$ that might be common components of the indeterminacy locus of all $f_{[2^m]P}$, $m \in \NN$, other codimension-two components of the indeterminacy locus of a particular $f_{[2^m]P}$ will never reappear as components of the indeterminacy locus of $f_{[2^\ell]P}$ for any $\ell > m$.
nodes.statement_short: State the plan: only finitely many codimension-two components can be common to all $f_{[2^m]P}$, and the others never recur.

nodes.name: Replace $P$ by $[N]P$ and introduce $S_P$, $S_{P'}$
nodes.statement: Since the canonical height is a quadratic form, we may replace $P$ by $[N]P$ in Theorem A. Given any $P \in E(K)$, we replace $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $\ref{LNS}$ to assure that $P_\G$ is not a singular point of $E_\G$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\G \neq H_\infty$. So if we let $S_P$ be the set of all $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H_\infty(\CQ)$ such that the specialized point $P_t$ is a singular point on the specialized fiber $E_t$, then $S_P$ is an algebraic set (since singularity is an algebraic property) of codimension at least two in $\PP^n\backslash H_\infty$. In addition, we note that $S_P$ is contained in the discriminant locus $\D_E=0$. Similarly, we may assume the same for the corresponding point $P'$ on the isomorphic curve $E'$ defined by equation $(\ref{WE'})$, i.e. $P'_\G$ is not a singular point of $E'_\G$ for all smooth hypersurfaces $\G \neq H'_\infty$ and $S_{P'}$ has codimension at least $2$ in $\PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H'_\infty(\CQ)$.
nodes.statement_short: Using Lemma 5 and quadraticity of the canonical height, arrange that $S_P$ and $S_{P'}$ have codimension at least two.

nodes.name: Containment of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ away from $H_\infty$
nodes.statement: As before, let $I_{f_P}$ be the indeterminacy locus of the rational map $f_P$ induced by $P$. Then for all $t \in \PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H_\infty(\CQ)$ that are not in $I_{f_P} \cup S_P$, $f_P(t)=P_t$ is well-defined and is not a singular point on the cubic curve $E_t$. By lemma \ref{DL} and induction on $m$, $f_{[2^m]P}(t)=\left( [2^m]P\right)_t=[2^m]P_t$ is well-defined for all $m \in \NN$. Thus, $$I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap \left(\PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H_\infty(\CQ) \right) \subset I_{f_P}\cup S_P, \qquad\text{ for all }m \in \NN.$$ The exact same argument works for $P'$ and so we also have $$I_{f_{[2^m]P'}} \cap \left(\PP^n(\CQ)\backslash H'_\infty(\CQ) \right) \subset I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_{P'}\qquad\text{ for all } m \in \NN.$$
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 4 and induction on $m$, off $H_\infty$ the indeterminacy loci of all $f_{[2^m]P}$ sit inside $I_{f_P} \cup S_P$.

nodes.name: Points on $H_\infty$ and the definition of $B_P$
nodes.statement:
For $$t=[0:1:*: \dots:*] \in \left(I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\CQ)ight)  ackslash H'_\infty(\CQ),$$ if $t

In particular, lemma ef{PL} implies that in fact $[2^m]P'$ is a point of order $2$ on $E'_t$. Thus, for $\ell > m$, $([2^\ell]P')_t=[2^\ell]P'_t=[2^{\ell-m}]\left([2^m]P'_tight)=O_{E'_t}$, which implies that $t$ is not in $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ by the contrapositive statement of lemma ef{PL}. Notice that we are left with $t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \cap H_\infty(\CQ)\cap H'_\infty(\CQ)$, which is an algebraic set of codimension at least $2$ in $\PP^n(\CQ)$. To summarize, we have shown that given $P\in E(K)$, by replacing $P$ by $[N]P$ as in Lemma $ef{LNS}$ if necessary, so that $P_\G$ and $P'_\G$ are not singular points of $E_\G$ and $E'_\G$ respectively for all smooth hypersurface $\G$, for any $m \in \NN$, if $$ t \in I_{f_{[2^m]P}} \quad	ext{and}\quad t 
otin I_{f_P} \cup I_{f_{P'}} \cup S_P \cup S_{P'} \cup (H_\infty(\CQ)\cap H'_\infty(\CQ)), $$ then for any $\ell>m$, $t 
ot \in I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$. In particular, if we let $$B_P:=\left\{ H_\infty\cap H'_\infty, \ 	ext{dimension-$(n-2)$ components of }I_{f_P}\cup I_{f_{P'}}\cup S_P\cup S_{P'} ight\}, $$then for any $m \in \NN$, if $C$ is a dimension-$(n-2)$ component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ that is not in $B_P$, then $C$ is not a component of $I_{f_{[2^\ell]P}}$ for all $\ell > m$.
nodes.statement_short: On $H_\infty \setminus H'_\infty$ Lemma 6 forces $[2^m]P'_t$ to be $2$-torsion, so such $t$ drop out for larger exponents; collect the survivors into $B_P$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3 to $[2^m]P$ and pass to the limit
nodes.statement: To complete the proof for Theorem A, we consider any smooth hypersurface $\G \subset \PP^n$ that is not a component of the discriminant locus, so $E_\G$ is an elliptic curve over $\CQ(\G)$. Furthermore, if $\G$ does not contain any subvariety in $B_P$, then we have just shown that $\G$ does not contain any codimension-two component of $I_{f_{[2^m]P}}$ for all big enough $m \in \NN$. So by lemma \ref{leh}, we have $$\frac{h_{E_\G}([2^m]P_\G)}{\deg \G}=\frac{h_{E_\G}(\left([2^m]P\right)_\G)}{\deg \G}= h_E([2^m]P) $$ for all big enough $m \in \NN$. Dividing this equation by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and then taking the limit $m\rightarrow \infty$ will give us Theorem A.
nodes.statement_short: For $\G$ avoiding $B_P$, Lemma 3 holds for all large $m$; divide by $3 \cdot 2^{2m}$ and let $m \to \infty$.

nodes.name: Case of non-zero $K/\CQ$-trace
nodes.statement: If the $K/\CQ$-trace of $E$ (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6) is non-zero, then by the constraint of dimension, the $K/\CQ$-trace of $E$ is a dimensional one abelian variety, i.e. $E$ is $K$-isomorphic to $E_0 \times_{\CQ} K$ for an elliptic curve $E_0/\CQ$. So there is a Zariski dense open subset $U^0 \subset \PP^n$ such that for all $t \in U^0(\CQ)$, the fibers $E_t$ are isomorphic to $E_0$, thus the specialization maps for $\s_t: E_0 \times_{\CQ} K \longrightarrow E_t$ are injective for all $t \in U^0(\CQ)$. So in particular, any curve $C \subset \PP^n$ of degree $d$ that does not lie in the complement of $U^0$ will satisfies Theorem B and their union is $\PP^n$.
nodes.statement_short: If the trace is non-zero then $E$ is a constant curve and every specialization is injective on a dense open set.

nodes.name: Zero trace: injectivity on torsion
nodes.statement: We now suppose that the $K/\CQ$-trace of $E$ is zero, which implies that $E(K)$ is finitely generated, a result due to Lang-N\'eron (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 2). For any non-zero $P=[x:y:z] \in E(K)$, the algebraic set $$ \{ t \in U(\CQ)\ | \ [x(t):y(t):z(t)]=\s_t(P)=O=[0:1:0] \}$$ has dimension at most $n-1$. Since the subgroup of torsion points $E(K)_{\text{tors}}$ is finite, so we may shrink $U$ by discarding finitely many subvarieties of dimension at most $n-1$ and assume that $$E(K)_{\text{tors}} \longrightarrow E_t(\CQ) $$ is injective for all $t \in U(\CQ)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lang-N\u00e9ron gives $E(K)$ finitely generated; shrink $U$ so that the finite torsion subgroup injects.

nodes.name: The canonical height pairings
nodes.statement: On the other hand, We will use the canonical height pairing to prove that the specialization map is injective on the free part of $E(K)$. The canonical height pairing on $E(K)$ is $$\< \cdot , \cdot \>_E : E(K) \times E(K) \longrightarrow \RR $$ $$\<P, Q\>_E \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E}(P+Q)-\hat{h}_{E}(P)-\hat{h}_{E}(Q) \right).$$ Likewise, for any smooth hypersurface $\G \subset \PP^n$ such that $E_\G$ is non-singular, the canonical height pairing on $E_{\G}(\CQ(\G))$ is $$\< \cdot , \cdot \>_{E_{\G}} : E_{\G}(\CQ(\G)) \times E_{\G}(\CQ(\G)) \longrightarrow \RR $$ $$\<P_{\G}, Q_{\G}\>_{E_{\G}} \longmapsto \frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{h}_{E_{\G}}(P_{\G}+Q_{\G})-\hat{h}_{E_{\G}}(P_{\G})-\hat{h}_{E_{\G}}(Q_{\G}) \right).$$ It is a standard result that these pairings are bilinear on the corresponding abelian groups.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the bilinear canonical height pairings on $E(K)$ and on $E_\G(\CQ(\G))$.

nodes.name: Positive definiteness and non-vanishing Gram determinant
nodes.statement: However, it is more subtle when it comes to positive definiteness on the free part of the abelian group. In general, $\< \cdot , \cdot \>_E$ is positive definite on the quotient of $E(K)$ by the subgroup generated by $E(K)_\text{tors}$ and $K/\CQ\text{-trace of }E(K)$ (\cite{LFD}, Chapter 6, Theorem 5.4). Since we assume that the $K/\CQ$-trace of $E$ is zero, it follows that $\< \cdot , \cdot \>_E$ is a positive definite bilinear form on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$. Let $P^1, \ldots, P^r$ be a set of generators for the free part of $E(K)$. The positive definiteness of the canonical height pairing on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$ implies that $$ \det \left(\<P^i, P^j\>_E\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0.$$
nodes.statement_short: Zero trace makes the pairing positive definite on $E(K)/E(K)_\text{tors}$, so the Gram determinant of generators is non-zero.

nodes.name: Transfer the determinant through Theorem A
nodes.statement: Let $B_E$ be the union of all $B_{P^i}$'s as in Theorem A, then $B_E$ is a finite set of codimension-two subvarieties such that for any smooth hypersurface $\G \neq H_\infty$ that does not contain any subvariety in $B_E$ and is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ (so that $E_\G$ is non-singular), then the equality in Theorem A holds for $P^1, \ldots, P^r$. By multilinearity of determinant, we have \begin{align*} \frac{\det \left( \<P^i_\G, P^j_\G\>_{E_\G} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}}{(\deg \G)^r} &=\det\left( \frac{\<P^i_\G, P^j_\G\>_{E_\G}}{\deg\G} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \\ &=\det \left(\<P^i, P^j\>_E\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}\\ &\neq 0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: With $B_E=\bigcup B_{P^i}$, Theorem A and multilinearity of the determinant transfer non-vanishing to $E_\G$.

nodes.name: The codimension-two set $S_E$ from Lemma 5
nodes.statement: On the other hand, lemma \ref{LNS} implies that there exist $N_1, \ldots, N_r$ such that the locus for which the specialization of any one of $[N_1]P^1, \ldots, [N_r]P^r$ is a singular point is of dimension at most $n-2$. So this locus contains only a finite number of subvarieties of dimension $n-2$ and we let $S_E$ be the set of all these codimension-two subvarieties. If $\PP^{n-1}\cong\G \subset \PP^n$ is a hyperplane such that $E_\G$ is non-singular, we can view $E_\G$ as as an elliptic curve defined over $\CQ(\PP^{n-1})$. Furthermore, if $\G$ does not contain any of the subvarieties in $S_E$, then lemma \ref{LNS} holds for $P^1_\G, \ldots, P^r_\G$ without the assumption that the reduced Weierstrass equation of $E_\G$ is minimal.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5 supplies a finite set $S_E$ of codimension-two subvarieties off which it survives without minimality.

nodes.name: Dimension reduction by hyperplane sections
nodes.statement_short: Good hyperplanes are Zariski dense in the dual space, so induct on the dimension down to $\PP^2$.

nodes.name: Reduction along smooth curves of degree $d$
nodes.statement: We continue to reduce the dimension to one as above but do not restrict ourselves to just hyperplanes, i.e. we can choose any smooth curve $C \subset \PP^2$ of degree $d$ not contained in the complement of $U$, not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ and does not contain subvarieties in $B_E$. The union of all such curves is the Zariski open set $\PP^2\backslash B_E$, because given any point $t \in \PP^2(\CQ)\backslash B_E$, we can always find a smooth curve $C/\CQ$ of degree $d$ such that it contains $t$ but not points in $B_E$ and it is not a component of the discriminant locus of $E$ and $\PP^2\backslash U$. With this construction, over these infinitely many curves $C$ of degree $d$, we have $\det \left( \<P^i_C, P^j_C\>_{E_C} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0$. By continuity of the determinant function and Silverman's theorem (\cite{SHS}, Theorem B), we conclude that $\det \left( \<{P^i_C}_t, {P^j_C}_t\>_{{E_C}_t} \right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r} \neq 0,$ for all $t \in C(\CQ)$ with large enough $h_C(t)$. This means that the specialized points ${P^1_C}_t, \ldots, {P^r_C}_t$ are $\ZZ$-linearly independent. Since we always choose the hyperplanes (or smooth curves in the last induction step) not being contained in the complement of $U$, the specialization maps for $t \in U(\CQ)$ commute with reduction maps as shown in Figure 1.
nodes.statement_short: Choosing good degree-$d$ curves in $\PP^2$ and applying Silverman's Theorem B keeps the Gram determinant non-zero for large $h_C(t)$.

nodes.name: Injectivity of $\s_t$ for large $h_C(t)$
nodes.statement: So for $t \in C(\CQ) \cap U(\CQ)$ with $h_C(t)$ large enough, we have injectivity of $\s_t$ on both the free part and the torsion points of $E(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Combining the free-part and torsion arguments gives injectivity off a set of bounded height.

nodes.name: Zariski density of the good curves by induction on $n$
nodes.statement: Lastly, we will prove by induction on $n$ that the union of all such curves in Theorem B is Zariski dense in $\PP^n$. We have just shown in the previous paragraph that the case $n=2$ is true. For $E/\CQ(\PP^n)$ in general with $n \geq 2$, we have shown that the set of hyperplanes $\G \subset \PP^n$ such that condition $(\ref{LIG})$ holds on $E_\G/\CQ(\G\cong \PP^{n-1})$ is Zariski dense in ${\PP^n}^*$, thus the union of all such $\G$ (call them good $\G$) is Zariski dense in $\PP^n$. By induction hypothesis, the union of curves satisfying Theorem B for $E_\G/\CQ(\G\cong \PP^{n-1})$ (call them good curves of degree $d$ for $\G$) is Zariski dense in $\G$. So the union $$ \bigcup_{\text{good $\G$}} \text{union of good curves of degree $d$ for $\G$}$$ is Zariski dense in $\PP^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $n$: good hyperplanes are dense in $\PP^n$ and, by hypothesis, good curves are dense in each of them.
